question.stem: An architect is evaluating `db.students.deleteMany({})`, `db.students.drop()`, and `db.dropDatabase()` for storage lifecycle management; which architectural trade-offs hold true (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.deleteMany({})` empties all documents from `students` while preserving secondary indexes and validation rules
options.B: `db.students.drop()` preserves secondary B-tree indexes while deleting only BSON documents
options.C: `db.students.drop()` removes the `students` collection and its indexes while leaving sibling collections in `schoolDB` untouched
options.D: `db.dropDatabase()` deletes only empty collections and refuses to run when documents exist
options.E: `db.dropDatabase()` purges the entire active database, including every collection, document, and index inside it

answer.explanation: `deleteMany({})` deletes all documents while keeping the collection and its indexes intact (A); `db.students.drop()` destroys the `students` collection, its documents, and its indexes without affecting sibling collections (C); and `db.dropDatabase()` permanently deletes the entire selected database and all of its collections (E). (Key Takeaway: Choose `deleteMany({})` to keep collection metadata, `drop()` to remove one collection, and `dropDatabase()` to purge the entire database.)

question.stem: Why would a query `db.students.find({ age: { $gt: 18, $lt: 15 } })` return zero documents even when the `students` collection contains thousands of records spanning ages 10 to 25 (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Because MongoDB syntax prohibits placing two comparison operators inside `{ age: { ... } }`
options.B: Because multiple conditions inside `{ age: { $gt: 18, $lt: 15 } }` are evaluated with implicit logical AND semantics
options.C: Because `$gt` and `$lt` automatically delete documents that fail the range check
options.D: Because no numeric `age` value can simultaneously be strictly greater than `18` and strictly less than `15`
options.E: Because `find()` requires `{ _id: 0 }` whenever range operators are used

answer.explanation: Placing multiple comparison operators on the same field (`{ age: { $gt: 18, $lt: 15 } }`) creates an implicit conjunction (AND) requiring both predicates to hold simultaneously (B). Since the interval $(18, 15)$ is mathematically empty, no scalar value can satisfy both `$gt: 18` and `$lt: 15` (D). (Key Takeaway: Inverted range bounds inside a single field filter create an unsatisfiable AND predicate.)

question.stem: A backend service executes `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $set: { age: 20 }, $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $push: { subjects: "History" } })`; which invariants govern this atomic operation (Select all that apply)?

options.A: If multiple documents have `name: "Rahul"`, only the first matching document is modified
options.B: The `age` field on the matched document is set to `20` without overwriting unreferenced fields
options.C: The numeric `attempts` field is incremented by `1` in the same atomic document mutation
options.D: The existing `subjects` array is overwritten so that `"History"` becomes its sole element
options.E: The string `"History"` is appended to the end of the `subjects` array

answer.explanation: `updateOne()` modifies only the first matching document (A), `$set` updates `age` to `20` in place (B), `$inc` adds `1` to `attempts` (C), and `$push` appends `"History"` to the `subjects` array without erasing prior array elements (E). (Key Takeaway: Multi-operator `updateOne()` calls apply `$set`, `$inc`, and `$push` atomically to the first matched document.)

question.stem: Which pagination pipelines correctly retrieve the 3rd page of results (where each page displays 5 students ordered from highest to lowest `grade`) (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.find().sort({ grade: 1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`
options.B: `db.students.findOne().sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`
options.C: `db.students.find({}).sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`
options.D: `db.students.find().sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(15).limit(5)`

answer.explanation: Calling `find()` or `find({})` returns a cursor over all documents; `.sort({ grade: -1 })` orders from highest to lowest `grade`; `.skip(10)` skips the first 2 pages (`10` records); and `.limit(5)` returns the 5 records on Page 3 (C, E). (Key Takeaway: Both `find()` and `find({})` match all documents and chain `.sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`.)

question.stem: An API endpoint must return a single student object (or `null`) matching `{ grade: { $gte: 8 } }` containing strictly the `name` field and no `_id` field; which query satisfies all constraints (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.find({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })`
options.B: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })`
options.C: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1 })`
options.D: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $gt: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })`

answer.explanation: `findOne()` returns a single document object (or `null`) instead of a cursor, `{ grade: { $gte: 8 } }` matches grade 8 or higher, and `{ name: 1, _id: 0 }` includes `name` while explicitly suppressing `_id` (B). (Key Takeaway: `findOne(filter, { name: 1, _id: 0 })` returns one document object projected to a single field.)

question.stem: Which statements accurately contrast implicit collection creation (via `insertOne()`) against explicit creation (via `db.createCollection(name, options)`) (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Explicit `db.createCollection(name, options)` allows pre-configuring JSON schema validation rules or capped collection sizes before any document is inserted
options.B: Implicit collection creation via `insertOne()` fails unless the parent database already has at least one other collection
options.C: Collections created via `db.createCollection("students")` remain invisible to `show collections` until `insertMany()` is called
options.D: Implicit creation via `insertOne()` or `insertMany()` requires zero prior schema declaration and creates the collection automatically on first write

answer.explanation: Explicit `db.createCollection(name, options)` is used when setting validation rules or a capped collection size ahead of time (A), while implicit creation automatically creates the collection on the first `insertOne()` or `insertMany()` call without prior schema setup (D). Note that explicitly created collections immediately appear in `show collections`. (Key Takeaway: Explicit `createCollection()` configures options like validation or capped size; implicit creation provisions standard collections on first insert.)

question.stem: Given a collection with documents `{ name: "Meera", age: 17 }`, `{ name: "Kabir", age: 18 }`, and `{ name: "Rahul", age: 19 }`, which queries match `Kabir` and `Rahul` while excluding `Meera` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.find({ age: { $lt: 18 } })`
options.B: `db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18 } })`
options.C: `db.students.find({ age: { $in: [18, 19] } })`
options.D: `db.students.find({ age: { $nin: [17] } })`

answer.explanation: Among ages 17, 18, and 19, `Kabir` (18) and `Rahul` (19) are matched while `Meera` (17) is excluded by `{ age: { $gte: 18 } }` (B), `{ age: { $in: [18, 19] } }` (C), and `{ age: { $nin: [17] } }` (D). Option A matches only `Meera`, and Option E excludes `Kabir`. (Key Takeaway: Equivalent result sets on finite domains can be expressed via `$gte`, `$in`, or `$nin`.)

question.stem: How do `$push` and `$pull` behave when modifying the `subjects` array inside `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, ...)` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ $push: { subjects: "History" } }` appends `"History"` to the `subjects` array
options.B: `{ $pull: { subjects: "Science" } }` deletes Rahul's entire document if `"Science"` is found in `subjects`
options.C: `{ $push: { subjects: "History" } }` removes all existing elements before inserting `"History"`
options.D: `{ $pull: { subjects: "Science" } }` decrements a numeric counter named `Science` by 1
options.E: `{ $pull: { subjects: "Science" } }` removes matching `"Science"` entries from the `subjects` array in place

answer.explanation: `$push` adds a value to an array field (A), whereas `$pull` removes matching instances of a value (`"Science"`) from an array field in place without deleting the enclosing document (E). (Key Takeaway: `$push` appends elements to an array; `$pull` removes matching elements from an array.)

question.stem: Which statements accurately evaluate compound logical filtering with `$and` and `$or` in MongoDB queries (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Both `$or` and `$and` accept an array of condition objects (`[{ ... }, { ... }]`) as their value
options.B: `$or` returns a document only when every condition object in its array is satisfied
options.C: `$and` is an update operator used inside `updateMany()` to combine `$set` and `$inc`
options.D: `db.students.find({ $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] })` matches documents satisfying either condition
options.E: `$and` evaluates to true only when all sub-clauses in its condition array match the document

answer.explanation: Logical operators `$or` and `$and` take an array of condition objects (A); `$or` evaluates to true when at least one sub-clause matches (D), and `$and` evaluates to true only when all sub-clauses match (E). (Key Takeaway: `$or` and `$and` combine arrays of filter objects using logical disjunction and conjunction.)

question.stem: When designing a high-reliability MongoDB CRUD data layer based on the VVIT reference manual, which operational principles always hold true (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Switching to a non-existent database via `use <dbName>` does not allocate disk files until data is written into a collection
options.B: `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` requires its multiple document payloads to be wrapped in an array
options.C: Calling `find()` returns a cursor supporting `.sort()`, `.skip()`, and `.limit()`, whereas `findOne()` returns a single document or `null`
options.D: Projection `{ field: 1 }` includes the field, `{ field: 0 }` excludes it, and `_id` is included by default unless `{ _id: 0 }` is specified
options.E: `deleteMany({})` removes all documents in a collection while keeping the collection container, whereas `db.<collection>.drop()` destroys the collection and its indexes

answer.explanation: All five statements represent foundational invariants across the VVIT MongoDB reference guide: lazy database creation on first write (A), array syntax for `insertMany()` (B), cursor vs. single-document semantics of `find()` vs. `findOne()` (C), projection inclusion/exclusion and default `_id` rules (D), and collection truncation (`deleteMany({})`) vs. collection drop (`drop()`) (E). (Key Takeaway: Mastering lazy allocation, batch arrays, cursor pipelines, `_id` projection rules, and truncation vs. dropping ensures sound MongoDB architecture.)
